speechtext:
Yes, $52.45 a month is what I should have said; taxes $20 a month; fire insurance, $1.50 a month; and the note says this $1.50 is a more considered opinion than was given in the two previous examples. The total charges on this mortgage would be $73.95 per month. The income required to carry such a mortgage at the 23 per cent ratio is $3,860 per annum. Those are the government's own figures. As I say, the income requirement of $3,860 has been worked out on the basis of a man being allowed to spend 23 per cent of his income on the carrying charges of his house.
83276-87J
National Housing Act
I say, Mr. Speaker, that if a man wants to spend more than 23 per cent of his income on the carrying charges of his house, that is his business. He should be allowed to do so. Who are we to tell a man how he is to spend his income? If a man wants to do without a car, or if he wants to do without a television set or the various other things that might be necessary to make it possible for him to pay considerably more than 23 per cent of his income toward the carrying charges of his home, I would say that is his decision to make. In addition to that there may easily be, and today generally are, other members of the family who are wage earners who would be glad to contribute toward the carrying charges of the house. Therefore I feel it is only reasonable and sensible to reduce the income requirement applying on Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation mortgages to $3,000 per year or $60 per week.
I feel that this change will make it possible for a great many people, who today cannot buy their own homes, to purchase homes. It will still leave more than half the people of Canada unable to buy homes. In order to overcome this problem I believe Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation must alter its -building specifications to allow less costly types of construction. I do not mean that we should allow contractors to build match boxes or inferior types of houses. I have been shown plans by builders which embodied attractive two-bedroom houses with living room, dining room, kitchen and -bathroom, as well as a full cellar. These contractors will be glad to sell these houses for $8,000 provided the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will alter the building specifications. These houses are no myth. They can be a reality. They are attractive. They simply do not contain some of the frills that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation now requires in houses under the National Housing Act.
These houses would not contain as much brick as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation houses do now. They would be of good, sturdy, attractive construction. They would last for many, many years. I believe it is important for us to make houses available to the working people of this country at less than today's cost. As I say, these houses would provide for families with one, two or three children, and would allow a man to carry the charges if he were earning about $2,500 per year. This would -bring into the field of potential purchasers a tremendous number of people who today want to buy their own homes and are prohibited from, doing so.

National Housing Act I believe the second requirement for us to catch up on our housing backlog is to make it possible for people to afford the down payment on a house. This bill provides for a down payment of 10 per cent on the first $8,000 loan and 30 per cent on the remainder. As I said earlier, the cheapest Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation house you can buy today costs $10,000, so the lowest down payment today would be $1,400. This is still beyond the reach of the man earning a moderate income.
Building costs are increasing steadily, and if the new act is to be effective for any length of time that down payment should be 10 per cent on all houses up to a value of $12,000. If building costs continue to increase, as they give every indication of continuing to increase, it will not be long before the cheapest house you can buy under the National Housing Act will cost $12,000.
In addition to the down payment, the amortization is a very important factor in making it possible for people with moderate incomes to buy new houses. Under this bill the amortization period has been lengthened to 25 years. I believe the amortization period should be lengthened to 30 years, because that would allow a great many more people to carry the charges on new houses than would otherwise be possible. It can be done without appreciably increasing the risk to the lender, because builders tell me that today Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation houses will last for anywhere from 50 to 70 years. If the amortization period is increased to 30 years, this will still leave the lender a generous margin of safety.
In order to show how the thinking has developed in the United States with regard to providing houses for low income groups, I should like to quote a dispatch which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of January 9, 1954, under the heading "Radical Plan for Home Owner Urged in United States". The dateline is Washington; it is an Associated Press dispatch, and reads as follows:
Senator Homer Capehart (Republican-Indiana) today suggested a $1,000,000,000 government program to help people buy homes on 50 to 60 year mortgages with little or no down payment.
Capehart, chairman of the Senate banking committee which will consider President Eisenhower's housing proposal advanced what he called a "radical idea" of making home owners of citizens otherwise unable to afford their own dwellings.
He told a CIO housing conference he had long been worried about the plight of citizens who cannot afford either a down payment on a home or "the high rents they are forced to pay today."
Capehart disapproved past programs under which public housing has been built with federal subsidies for rent to low income families. He said it would be better to help such families finance their own homes.

I think that dispatch is particularly interesting, owing to the fact it is not the statement of any airy dreamer but is made by the chairman of the United States banking committee, the man who will be given responsibility for putting through President Eisenhower's housing program. It shows how far thinking along these lines has developed in the United States. I do not agree with the suggestions he has made, but I think it makes the suggestions I am making, and the other suggestions I am about to make, seem very moderate indeed.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, in addition to making it possible for people to buy houses, it is very important that the necessary mortgage money to finance the construction of those new houses be made available. Under the provisions of the bill, banks will be permitted to deal in housing mortgages under an insurance scheme whereby the government will guarantee the mortgage. At first sight this would seem to make sufficient additional mortgage money available, but it seems to me one important factor has been overlooked.
I have talked very recently with senior officials of two of our largest banks, and they have both told me that that part of their investment portfolios which they are permitted to invest in non-government securities is almost completely taken up with investments in commerce and industry.
If we are going to close the gap between mortgage money now available and mortgage money that is needed it seems to me, as it seemed to them, that some of the money which is at present being invested in commerce and industry will have to be diverted from those fields so it can be used for housing mortgages. This, of course, is going to slow down commercial and industrial development, upon which our whole economy depends. And if that kind of slow-down, which certainly we can ill afford, is to be avoided, the government must tell the people of Canada, and particularly the banks involved-because they do not know it yet-where these additional funds are to come from. We will be listening attentively to learn this from the minister, when he decides to tell us.
Another aspect of the matter, with which I heartily disagree, is the fact that the banks are not going to carry out their own appraisals and inspections. These tasks are going to be carried out for them by officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This will give the government control over a very large proportion of the mortgage and lending operations connected with the building industry, and will place the government in an entrenched position, so far as that industry is concerned.

After all, the government is guaranteeing these bank loans. Therefore I can see no reason at all why the banks should not be ready, willing and anxious to bear the cost of their own appraisals and inspections, just as the other lending institutions that have been participating with the government in the building of houses over the past few years have been willing to bear the cost of carrying out their own appraisals and inspections.
I believe the banks should be instructed by the government right now to begin training the staffs they will require so that, in a minimum of time, they will be ready to function. I believe the eagerness-and there can be no doubt that there has been great eagerness on the part of the government in this respect-to take over appraisals and inspections from the banks is simply another demonstration of the government's intention to go on assuming more and more control over as many as possible of the proper functions of industry.
It seems to me that this is simply another example of this government's drift toward socialism, a government which is so fond of professing its adherence to the principles of free enterprise. I sincerely hope the banks will stand up to the government and insist upon doing their own appraisals and inspections, because that is the only way we can stop this drift of the government toward getting into business. My view is that so far as possible the government must be kept out of business, and I sincerely hope the banks will not permit the government to bulldoze them any further. I hope they will stand up to the government and say, "We want to do our own inspections and appraisals."
I believe that if the government insists upon doing appraisals and inspections it will reduce almost to the vanishing point the effectiveness of the 4,000 branch banks about which the minister spoke so glibly when he dealt with the matter in the house last December. It is obvious that if appraisals and inspections have to be carried out by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, a branch bank can be only as effective as the service it can get from the nearest Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation official.
I would say that if the government insists upon doing this work, then it might just as well go whole hog. It is guaranteeing the loans anyway, so it might as well go whole hog and make the mortgages available to the people who want them for the purpose of building houses. If it did this it could make mortgage money available at 4J per cent. The government pays to the people of Canada a rate of 3| per cent. Add half of one per
National Housing Act
cent, the cost of servicing a mortgage, and you have the 4J per cent. It must be one thing or the other; either bring the banks in and let them do the job completely, or else stop this farce and keep the banks out, and let the government do the job. Let us have it one way or the other.
I believe, really, that the only reason the banks are being brought into the picture is that the government wants the banks to do the dirty work when people have to be evicted from their homes. It seems very clear to me that when the nice things are going to be done, such as approving a loan, the government wants to be on hand with the smiles and chuckles, saying, "Oh, yes, here is your nice home, Mr. Smith. We are very glad to give you a mortgage, and it is only going to cost you so much. Just sign on the dotted line, and don't forget to vote Liberal next time you go to the polls, because, remember, we are doing it for you."
Then when that poor, unfortunate man- and there will be some-has to default in his payments, is the government going to go to him and say, "We are sorry, Mr. Smith, but you cannot stay in your house." Oh, no, the poor old bank has to do that; it then becomes the villain in the piece. The banker is the one who is hated by the person evicted. The whole thing becomes a farce: the government does all the nice things, and the bank does all the nasty things. The government carries out all inspections, and proceeds to kid itself and the people of Canada that the branch banks will be effective. Well, the branch banks will be only as effective as their nearness to an office of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. That is why I think this whole thing is a gigantic bluff, trying to kid the people into believing that they are going to be able to get houses cheaper and easier than they did before.
So much for that. I hope the government is going to pay some attention to some of these suggestions, because I believe the very best investment we can make in good citizenship is to make it as easy as possible for a man to own his own home. The home owner has a stake in the community, and I believe we will all agree he becomes the best possible kind of citizen. That is the greatest possible bulwark we can have against the inroads of communism.
In addition to the shortage of houses a person may buy, there is also an acute shortage of rental housing. Very little is available at reasonable rentals. A few weeks ago in Toronto I went to see a house put up by the Toronto metropolitan home builders' association. This house was erected to show

National Housing Act
what the industry can do on a non-subsidized basis to provide the kind of rental housing people need at rentals they can pay.
This house is designed to meet the needs of people with one, two or three children, and earning between $2,500 and $3,500 a year. It is 18 feet wide and 23 feet deep. It has a front lawn, a back garden, two storeys and a basement. On the top floor there are two bedrooms and a three-piece bathroom. On the ground floor there is a living room, dining room and kitchen. The basement is full size with a coal furnace, hot water heater and laundry tubs.
The whole design of this house is most attractive. It gives you the impression it has been well thought out. It is well finished and very attractive to the eye. The floors throughout the house are hardwood with the exception of the bathroom and kitchen floors, which are of linoleum tile. The Toronto metropolitan home builders' association plans to rent this house at $58 a month; and on the basis of a man being allowed to spend 23 per cent of his income on shelter, this kind of accommodation can be carried by a man earning $55 a week.
During the first few days this rental unit was open for inspection more than 5,000 couples signed cards saying they were very anxious to have the opportunity of renting this kind of accommodation at $58 a month. The majority of the people who thought this type of accommodation was attractive were earning between $2,500 and $3,500 a year, and had two children. When I was there I listened to the comments made by the people going through, and they were frankly comments of amazement that such accommodation could be made available at a rental of $58 a month.
This kind of accommodation is in very sharp contrast to the single rooms in which families with four or five children are living today in Toronto, and I am sure in other centres throughout Canada, and for which they are paying as high as $60 a month rent. They are living in such accommodation simply because they cannot find anywhere else to go, and they live in constant fear that they are going to be evicted because of the children. I believe this type of project is a very good example of how the needs of people can be met by industry if industry gets down to the job, and remember that is on a non-subsidized basis. This kind of project is completely non-subsidized.
To make the project a reality the government must make available to those who will carry out the construction, money for land and construction at an interest rate of 3f
TMr. Hees.]
per cent. I know the minister is going to say that money is available at that interest rate if the company is a limited dividend corporation. However, I see no reason why this interest rate should be confined to limited dividend corporations which are restricted to a return of 5 per cent on their investment, because we all know that if you have money to invest you can get better than 5 per cent today with very great security by putting your money into any good industrial common stock.
Therefore I say that if a co-operative effort like this can make available to people, in large quantities, the kind of rental housing they are anxious to obtain at a rental they are able to pay, then the government, on inspection and after satisfying themselves that the rent is fair for the accommodation which will be afforded, should make money available for construction at 3? per cent. It makes money available at the same rate of interest to housing projects that need a subsidy to enable them to pay their way, and it is the rate of interest which the government pays the people of Canada for the use of their money. I cannot think of any better way that money can be spent to good account.
Finally, I believe this legislation can be made effective if the following requirements are complied with. First of all, I think the income requirement to obtain an N.H.A. mortgage must be reduced to $3,000 a year. Second, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation building specifications should be eased to permit a less costly type of construction which will make low-priced houses available to people in the low income brackets. Third, the down payment should be reduced to a flat 10 per cent on all N.H.A. houses up to a value of $12,000. Fourth, the period over which the loan can be paid off should be lengthened to 30 years. Fifth, the government must make it clear, in the very near future, where the money necessary to finance additional mortgages is going to come from without depriving commerce and industry of the funds being invested in those fields at the present time. Sixth, I believe the government must make funds available at 3f per cent to low-rental housing projects which do not require a subsidy, and which provide the type of rental housing that people want, at rents which they can pay.
If these six conditions are complied with, this legislation can materially help us to catch up on our ever-increasing backlog of half a million houses.

The difference between a mortgage at 5 per cent and one at 6 per cent is only slightly less than 5 years of mortgage payments. Thus we see the vital role played by interest in the financing of home purchases.
Hence any benefits under the new bill in so far as a lower down payment and increased amortization period are concerned will not bring the most desirable results if the government fails to lower the interest rate. I will grant you that under the new bill some people will be able to purchase homes who might not ordinarily have been able to do so, but it must be remembered that in many cases they are going to have to pay more as a result of the longer period of repayment on the loan.
We of the C.C.F. have always advocated a lower interest rate because we believe that it is only through a lower interest rate that we can make it possible for a great number of Canadians to undertake the purchase of their own homes. A low rate of interest is a vital part of any housing program, and the lack of that low rate is perhaps the most glaring inadequacy in the present legislation.
As regards the insurance aspects of this bill, section 40 of the old act contained an insurance feature which, although very limited in scope, was not designed to operate at the expense of the borrower. Under the new act the prospective home owner will have to pay not only what we consider to be an exorbitant rate of interest but in addition an insurance premium which in some instances, since the insurance may be capitalized into the mortgage loan and amortized accordingly, may mean an increase of two-tenths of one per cent which, of course, will be added to the already high rate of interest.
I was very interested in the comments made in regard to free enterprise by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees). It has always interested me to hear comments by various members of the house about the virtues of free enterprise. But I have always understood that the reason the lenders were able to charge the high rate of interest was because they were lending their money at a risk. In other words, it was risk capital. If a man had money and he made it available to others then he risked that money, and was therefore entitled to a high interest rate or profit.
The situation we now face is that the government is taking away the risk and at the same time permitting lending institutions to exact the profits. Under this legislation

the government is stepping in and assuming the risk at the borrower's expense, while at the same time permitting the private lending institutions to take the profit. There can be no excuse whatsoever for a provision of this nature in this legislation.
It is rather amusing at times to hear the comments made regarding paternalism and the way in which people attempt to disparage the idea of the welfare state. They take exception to members of this group asking for increases in old age pensions or family allowances. They are prone to criticize us for being paternalistic and for going out of our way to help various sections of our population. But the amazing thing is this. They are glad to help out those who in the main require no help whatsoever. I have noticed that the larger a company is in this country the more likely it is to run to the government for help any time it gets into difficulties. Many of the bigger industries in this country have for many years enjoyed some form of government protection, yet these same people see nothing wrong with that. It is all very well for private enterprise to come running to the government for assistance, but it is a different story altogether when people who want to purchase homes ask for some assistance from this government.
The hon. member for Broadview suggested that this legislation was placing more power in the hands of the government. We feel the contrary is true, and what is actually happening is that the government is getting out of the lending field and turning over to private enterprise the last interest it had in housing. The government is doing that after having guaranteed the profits of private enterprise through the insurance scheme.
I find it difficult to understand the point of view of those who claim the government is taking too much upon itself at the expense of private enterprise. On this point there is one question I would like to direct to the minister, and I hope he will be able to give the house the information when he rises to close the debate. I wonder how important this insurance feature is, and I would ask the minister to inform the house how many mortgages under the old N.H.A. went into default over the past five years. If he can demonstrate that over the past five years a large percentage of the mortgages arranged under the old N.H.A. went into default, then he may at least have some pretext for advancing this insurance feature at this time. But I am doubtful that that has been the case. Perhaps the government is worried about a recession, or perhaps it is afraid of 83276-88
National Housing Act
a slump. That would seem to me to be the only logical reason for inserting this feature into the act.
We have often been accused of being a group of crepe hangers and spreaders of gloom because we dared to suggest we ought to be planning for the future and taking care we do not once again find ourselves in the position we found ourselves in before the last war. I think the government ought to take the people into its confidence. Are they afraid of a drop in real estate values? Are they afraid of a slump? Is that the reason for the insertion of this insurance feature in this bill? That seems to me to be the only logical reason for adopting that feature at this time.
It will be interesting to learn how many mortgages went into default over the past five years, because the insurance companies have invested just under 20 per cent of their assets in mortgages. Under the new provisions of this bill it is unlikely the banks will be investing more than 5 per cent of their assets in real estate mortgages. These mortgages, of course, will be accepted as security by the Bank of Canada just in the same manner as government bonds. I find it difficult to understand why the government saw fit to place this burden on those who wish to buy homes, by requiring them to pay an insurance policy to protect not their own investment but the investment of the lending institution. If these people believe in free enterprise let them take the risk. That is the test.

In the final analysis the effectiveness of this act will be determined by the number of people whom it affects. Some reference was made to this matter by the last speaker. I wonder how many people in Canada will derive direct benefit under this new housing legislation. Obviously this bill is designed to meet the needs of those who have incomes of between $3,500 and $4,000 a year or more. The last speaker gave a figure of, I believe,

What is the situation? I went to the last available Canada Year Book and looked up the statistics with regard to income tax returns. This is what I find in 1950, the last year for which I have figures. I may say that it is not the amount of the figures but rather the relative number in each of the categories that is pertinent to this point. In the year 1950 I find that, of those paying income tax in Canada, there were 5,450 Canadians making income tax returns with incomes of less than $1,000. What is in the new act for them? I find that there were 740,070 taxpayers reporting incomes of $1,000 and up to but not including $2,000. What is in the legislation for them? I find that there were 848,960 Canadian citizens making income tax returns and reporting incomes from $2,000 up to but not including $3,000. I find that of those earning incomes between $3,000 and $3,500 there were an additional 243,000 Canadians, making a grand total of

That number represents a little more than 80 per cent of the population of this country. Eighty per cent of the people of this country are earning incomes of $3,500 or less. Let us go down a little bit to those earning incomes of $3,000 or less. I find that a total of

What, may I ask, is in the act for them? What is this new National Housing Act doing for 80 per cent of our people? Assuming that some of the people at the very top with regard to income will have no need to ask the government for any form of assistance, I think it will be seen that it is reasonable to propose that not more than one-fifth of the people of this country will ever be in a position to avail themselves of any opportunities or benefits under this act.
Surely the test of a good piece of legislation is that it should take care of the needs of the majority of our people, and certainly of the needs of those people who are least able to take care of themselves. But what does this act do? As other hon. members have suggested, it shows more concern for those who perhaps can do something for themselves, and shows very little concern indeed for those who can do nothing for themselves. I suggest that the minister and the government explain why they have seen fit to ignore completely the needs of the vast majority of the Canadian people in this regard.
IMr. Ellis.]

In connection with the situation throughout Canada there are many other statistics available. I was reading a copy of a brief submitted by a welfare council in the city of Montreal just a year and a half ago, which reported that about 70 per cent of the people 'of Montreal were earning less than $2,000 a year. I must take that figure as being fairly accurate. I think the social welfare people, such as the Red Feather agencies, are in a position to know the situation fairly well in their respective communities. When we realize the tremendous need for housing in this country, how can we be content when we find the government getting up and patting themselves on the back because they are advancing a piece of legislation that completely ignores four-fifths of the people of this country? We have suggested that this legislation should be changed in order to take care of the needs of those people who most need help. I suggest that we are not the only ones to suggest that it is time the government took some step in this regard and was prepared to do a little bit toward subsidizing home construction, if necessary.
I was interested in going back and reading an editorial that appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of April 9 of last year. It commented on the 600 applications which had been received for the 58 units of the Lowren Housing Company in the city of Ottawa. The editorial went on to say that under this scheme rentals were to be $55 a month and that no one earning more than $3,500 a year and having less than two children under 16 years of age would be eligible for such a house. But the editorial went on to point out that families earning less than $3,000 a year could not be expected to occupy such homes because they could not afford them. The Citizen went on to state:
Such families need to be subsidized if they are to obtain adequate accommodation.
I do not think the Citizen is a spokesman for our group but I believe it is expressing what is felt by a great many Canadian people who maintain that it is time the government faced up to the housing problem in this country. I was also interested in noting an editorial that appeared in a financial journal which reached my desk the other day, namely the Financial Times of January 22 of this year. In this editorial the writer quotes from an address given by Mr. B. S. Vanstone, president of the Bank of Toronto. I am going to quote an excerpt from this bank president's address. The editorial states as follows:
Dealing with this subject in the course of his address to the annual meeting of the Bank of

Toronto, B. S. Vanstone, president of that institution, stated that it is right and proper that the maximum number of Canadians should live in their own homes. But, he emphasized, this they can do only if construction and financing costs remain within their capacity to pay. If, he said, the need for extra houses in Canada is considered so pressing that private capital cannot be marshalled quickly enough to meet it, "then presumably public funds will have to be made available;" . . .
I do not think we are hearing from a socialist there, when he suggests that if private capital will not do the job, the government should step in and do something to correct this deplorable situation in the country.
As to this legislation, I feel that the government is looking at the entire problem of housing through the glasses of the private lending institutions and not from the viewpoint of the vast number of Canadian citizens who desire either to own their own homes or to obtain suitable rental accommodation. When the private lending institutions think of housing, what do they think of? They think of ways of increasing the flow of capital into housing, and they think in terms of increased interest rates. As a matter of fact, yesterday I was reading a little item in the Financial Post which suggested that the assumed solution to the problem of mortgage money is to increase the interest rate and to increase government guarantees.
That is precisely what this government have done in this legislation. They have given the private lending institutions a guaranteed return on their capital. They have removed all risk. Then, to add insult to injury, they have added the cost of protecting the private lending institutions to the other costs payable by the home purchaser.
We in this group have maintained throughout that we must look upon housing as a social problem and that we must get away from this feeling that the only way we can get houses built in this country is by going down on our hands and knees and begging the private lending institutions to come in with their money.
We go to the extent of guaranteeing their investments. Surely, if we consider the social implications of housing, we realize that poor housing has had a great effect on juvenile delinquency; it has had a great effect on domestic difficulties throughout the country, and it has had a great influence on our crime rate. We are told that is so by people who have made a study of these important problems. Surely the time has come for the government to consider housing from that viewpoint and be prepared, if necessary, to provide subsidized housing.

We are not the only ones in the country to suggest subsidized housing. The government chooses to ignore the representations made to it in many instances by people who would normally support the government. When the minister makes his reply at the end of the debate I wish he would tell the house why he considers that, when the government ignores the vast majority of the Canadian people, he can claim that this housing bill is any great boon to this country.
If this bill will enable one more house to be built, it is all right in so far as it goes. I suppose we should be thankful for small mercies. If it will enable one more house to go up, it is better than the old bill; it is better than nothing. But if the members of this government feel they can stick out their chests and brag about what they are doing for housing, and if this bill is what they feel will serve the needs of the Canadian people, then I suggest they are going to be in for a rude awakening.
It is all very well for some hon. members to say that people should make a down payment. I know many of my constituents, Mr. Speaker, who are living in rented dwellings. Some of them are paying $100 per month while they are earning $50 per week. How can they be expected to save money in that situation? It is all very well for some people to say they should be saving money, and perhaps 20 years from now these people might have the down payment on a home. In the meantime many of them are paying twice as much rent as they should be paying if they were buying their own homes.
So long as these people are forced to continue paying exorbitant rents, I ask in all sincerity how you can expect them to save the down payment on a home. I was talking to one gentleman some time ago and he said that it was quite true the new homes were expensive and beyond the reach of the average wage earner, but one had to remember that when people move into better homes they leave other homes for the people with lower incomes. What this man overlooked was that even if better housing is available, the time will come when a person who has the opportunity to move into better accommodation cannot afford it.
I wonder how many people who are living in tenements today, perhaps at very low rentals, are in a position to move into a suite at $85 per month if they had the chance. There are vast numbers of people in this country, as the Ottawa Citizen pointed out, on low incomes who, even if

National Housing Act
these rental dwellings at $55 a month were made available, would not be able to afford them.
I have made these comments on this bill because I believe it will be a cruel and bitter disappointment to the people of this country. It is a mirage. This measure was announced with great fanfare. When I went home for Christmas some of my constituents were saying they would now be able to build a house. When the time comes to enter into negotiations and have the lending value of the building established, these people will find out this legislation is not all it is cracked up to be. It is going to prove to be a bitter disappointment to many of our people. We are opposed to that.
I do not want to take up any more of the time of the house, but I do want to sum up by pointing out that we are disappointed with this legislation because it completely ignores the housing needs of the vast majority of the people of Canada.

I rise at this time, Mr. Speaker, to take part in this debate. I wish to emphasize at the outset that I support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) this afternoon concerning the revolving fund. I believe the suggestion is sound. The fund could be administered with a very small interest payment which, in reality, would amount to nothing more nor less than administration costs. I agree with him, and I believe that is not only one of the easiest ways of solving this problem, but it would be less expensive and less burdensome upon those who are desirous of obtaining their own homes. I support that suggestion, and I believe we shall have to keep harping on that proposal until the government sees fit to introduce some such measure.
In spite of what I may say this afternoon, I want it understood that we are desirous of doing everything possible to enable people to own their own homes. If this legislation is going to make that possible, then we are all for it. But I rather agree with many of the speakers who have preceded me that eventually the measure will result in disappointment. Once again, however, I wish to say that we are all for legislation that will enable our people to own their own homes. Personally-and I am speaking personally now-I am not so sure that that is the main objective of this bill. I have given this matter a good deal of thought, and I rather suspect there is another purpose behind this bill. I am going to explain exactly what I mean by that.
Throughout the war years and since the war there has been an inflationary trend. There

has been an expansion in the money supply of this country. Of course there is bound to be a limit to which the banking institutions can go in increasing that money supply or what is usually known as the expansion of credit. Sometimes these terms are not completely understood. I would prefer, instead of using the term "expansion of credit", that the term "expansion of the money supply of Canada" should be used. There must be a certain limit to that; otherwise the expansion is going to exceed by far the total price of the production and inflation will get out of hand. There must also be a time when that inflationary trend must stop; and when that happens the reverse action is likely to take place. Instead of the inflationary period simply stopping it takes the opposite trend, and we would be in for a period of deflation which, of course, would mean a recession.
I believe the government sees that in the offing, and is coming to this conclusion. "We must be careful in this matter. Otherwise there will not be an adequate supply of money, and therefore we must do something about it". The banking institutions will say, "We have to be careful here, too. We cannot expand beyond a limit which would be dangerous for us." And so the government says simply, "Here is a way in which you can continue to expand the money supply of the country and, at the same time, be insured against losses."
I agree fully with the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis), who preceded me in the debate, when he said that it is the home buyer who is going to pay for the insurance against any risk that might be involved. I believe that is one of the chief purposes behind the bill.
No one wants to see another depression; and I think by the proper application of financial policy there is no need to fear a depression. If the government persists in pursuing the policy it has been following, then of course it must do something to bolster the situation, and must attempt to stave off any possibility of depression.
Much has been said by the minister and by others who have spoken in the debate about the vast amount of savings on deposit in the banks. They have suggested that therefore the banks should be given added power to lend these savings. I rise now to refute a misconception in the minds of some in respect of that kind of argument. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) has already said that the method behind the bill is an inflationary one, and he has pointed out that the banks do not lend their depositors' money. It is not proper to say that it is time the vast

amount of savings on deposit in the banks was placed on loan, because I repeat the banks do not lend their depositors' money.
I know the opposite view is held by many people. Indeed, this is sometimes taught in our schools. Before my boys passed out of high school they used to come home and tell me that their teachers and principals had taught them that the banks lend depositors' money. It is also being taught in some universities. I have met men with bachelor of commerce degrees who have told me that the banks lend their depositors' money.
Not so long ago in this House of Commons the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Made-leine (Mr. Cannon), speaking in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, referred to the government's intention to introduce this bill. The rules do not permit my quoting from Hansard from a previous debate but, in substance, he said that a great pool of savings was available. I remember his use of that phrase; in fact I wrote out the quotation which, under the rules, I am not allowed to quote. I do remember, however, that he made reference to the great pool of savings in the banks, and suggested that they should be permitted to lend them.
The hon. member is not a dunce by any means. I have not looked up his-

On a recent occasion when the minister was speaking in the city of Toronto, he did hold out the hope that, without trespassing upon their existing volume of loans and investments for other purposes, the banks would have available a volume of funds arising from new deposits as the population increased.
Here he is quoting the minister himself, but I think he is quoting him with some degree of approval. A little further on in his speech he said:
I know we can assume that the banks will co-operate; but I hope we are not going to contemplate any pressures being exerted upon the Canadian banks to put depositors' money into longterm investments on mortgages under this act . . .
I would take it from that that the hon. member believes that banks lend their depositors' money. A little further on in his speech he said:
But let us recall, sir, that even though security is provided in that way, that in itself does not provide liquidity, because after all you can have a bank mortgage guaranteed against default, but if the mortgage goes on without default on the part of the mortgagor, the banks' funds are tied up. And they are tied up for periods up to 30 years, under the provisions of the new scheme.
I quote that because I should like to suggest to hon. members that it is not so much that depositors' money is tied up for that number of years as it is the collateral which the banks hold.
I want to refer to the minister's speech, and in doing so I am going to suggest that it is a little bit ambiguous on this point. I am saying it is ambiguous because that is the best way I can possibly give the minister some credit for, shall I be mean enough to say, knowing what he is talking about. But I am going to quote the minister, and if he means by his statement that the banks lend their depositors' money then he is wrong. If he means something else I would be happy to learn from him just what he does mean in

National Housing Act
order to clarify the situation. Let me read what the minister said, as found at page 1314 of Hansard for yesterday:
It is quite clear that if there is to be an increase in private lending additional funds must come from somewhere other than the present sources of institutional mortgage funds. The only other source of significant size stems from that part of the personal savings of individuals which year by year flows into savings deposits with the chartered banks. It is realized that at the present time these deposits are rather fully employed in other directions but we must remember that in conditions of normal growth in Canada there should be a substantial annual increase in savings deposits. Under our present laws these funds cannot move into the housing sector because the Bank Act prohibits bank lending on the security of real estate mortgages.
That is the part that is slightly ambiguous to my mind. Does the minister mean that these savings held by the people on deposit in banks are what the banks will lend if the Bank Act is changed to permit them to do so? If that is what he means, then I think he is wrong. Let me go on with what he said and then amplify it a little bit.
It is important to remember that the chartered banks perform in Canada a function with respect to savings that in other countries is performed not only by the banks, but also by building societies, mutual savings banks and savings and loan institutions.
This quotation indicates to me that the minister is of the opinion that the banks lend their depositors' money. I continue:
Because of the dominant position of the chartered banks in the savings field in Canada, and because mortgage lending is prohibited by the Bank Act, the housing sector is denied access to a large part of the funds which in other countries are available to finance home building.
Once again, I say it would appear to me that the minister is suggesting that the banks actually lend their depositors' money, which is not true. But if the minister intends instead to convey the idea that the banks must increase their cash reserves with the Bank of Canada so they will be enabled to expand the money supply of Canada by way of loans, then I would agree with him. But I do not quite read that in his speech. However, he can correct me on that point if he wishes.
It is one minute to six, Mr. Speaker, and we must go; but I am going to suggest that when I return I will read from the banking and commerce committee report of 1939 some evidence on this very point given by perhaps one of the greatest authorities in Canada, none other than the governor of the Bank of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the dinner recess at six o'clock I was attempting to expound what I felt to be the object behind this measure for national housing. I had indicated that I thought the object was to retain to some extent the present inflationary trend; that the government were perhaps much concerned lest we should go into a state of recession by reason of the calling in of bank loans, and they felt one way to avoid that was to bring in a measure such as this in order to permit the banking institutions to lend money on mortgages.
In making those points I referred to several speeches that had been made in the house and to a press clipping which indicated that many were of the opinion that the chartered banks loaned their depositors' money. I referred to a little article which appeared some weeks ago in the Ottawa Sentinel, and I suggested that the editor of the Sentinel also indicated that he believed that the banks loaned their depositors' money. I quoted from that article, and after six o'clock one of my colleagues reminded me that while it was quite possible that one could get that impression from the article, at the same time the editor of the Sentinel may have realized something that was more or less hidden behind the lines of that article. May I repeat what the editor said:
The only way they could enter the home mortgage business on a worth-while level would be by calling in existing loans.
The thought he may have intended to express was that the banks had almost reached the limit of their expansion, that is ten to one, and in order to go any further, which they were not permitted to do by the law unless they increased their cash reserve, they would have to call in some loans in order to continue their method of financial expansion. I make that possible correction because I want to be fair in my appraisals of quotations.
When we adjourned for the dinner recess it will be recalled that I had indicated I would bring to the house some authentic information which would refute any idea whatsoever that the banks loaned the savings of their depositors. I should like to refer now to evidence taken by the banking and commerce committee of this house in 1939. In the first instance I shall quote questions put to Mr. Towers, the governor of the Bank of Canada, who I think we must accept as an authority on these matters, by Mr. Jaques, who was then a member of this house. I

quote from page 455 as follows, where they were talking about the banks lending the savings of the depositors:
Q. I understood you to say they could not loan what did not belong to them.-A. The banks, cannot, of course, loan the money of their depositors. What the banks have done is to make loans and investments which result in a certain sum total of deposits.
For the sake of brevity I do not think I need read any further. Then follows an expansion of that idea. The point I wanted to bring forth was that the governor of the Bank of Canada said that the banks cannot of course loan the money of their depositors. At page 398 Mr. McGeer put the following question:
Q. So that if they have got up to the point where they have got bank deposits to lend-
It would appear as though at this point the governor of the Bank of Canada sort of butted in without waiting until Mr. McGeer completed his question, because he went on to say:
A. Well, they do not lend their deposits, of course.
That is pretty specific. Then I should like to quote from page 238 where the questions are being asked by Mr. Landeryou. I might point out that with the exception of Mr. McGeer it was Social Crediters who were asking these questions. I quote:
Q. Now, if the government went to the bank with $1,000,000 in bonds there would be an increase of $1,000,000 in the amount of money in the hands of the people in the form of deposits?-A. Assuming that no other change had taken place in the bank's position at that time, yes.
Q. In other words, when the $1,000,000 worth of bonds is presented to the bank a million dollars of money or the equivalent is created?-A. Again assuming that there is no decrease in its other investments or loans.
Q. I mean at the time, at the moment.-A. Yes.
Q. It is a fact that a million dollars of new money is created?-A. That is right. Of course, governments should not always go to banks in that connection; they should sell their bonds to investors.
That is true. That is what the government was doing throughout the time of war, but the result has not been very different because when they went to the people to ask them to buy bonds, the people in turn went to the banks to borrow money and the banks took the bonds as collateral and then issued new money by way of the loans, and the credit of the country was thus expanded.

That should settle the argument, but I doubt whether it will. I am quite certain that if the same discussion comes up at the next session somebody is bound to bob up and say that the banks lend their depositors' money. They do not; they issue freshly-created money. That is the method of expansion by the banks.
I would like to refer once again to the remarks made yesterday by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) because he made a point I thought was rather well taken in this connection, although I believe the hon. member is still under the impression that the banks lend their depositors' money. But here are the remarks of the hon. member as they appear on page 1329 of Hansard for January 21, 1954:
It is one thing, sir, to expand credit on commercial loans for a period, we will say, of nine months, but it is another thing to expand credit on mortgages having a lifetime of 25 or 30 years. In other words, it is an entirely new field so far as the banks are concerned.
The point the hon. member has made is to my mind the reason why the insurance scheme was written into the legislation. A period of 25 or 30 years is a long time to continue this expanded credit, because there is another side to this picture, namely that while the banks create new money every time they make a loan, that new money becomes the deposits of the people. These deposits, or savings if you will, in turn become a liability as far as the banks are concerned, because they have to pay that money out on demand. While it is true the banks, in making loans, release a fresh supply of money created out of nothing, these loans become deposits and automatically become liabilities to the banks. If the banks have to meet these liabilities over a period of 25 or 30 years then I personally do not blame them for saying, "If you want us to do that you had better guarantee us against loss". After all, their depositors and they themselves must be protected though, as previous speakers have emphasized, the government in providing that protection has made the prospective home owner pay the shot.
I have been dwelling on this matter of savings, and it may perhaps be presumed there are large savings deposits in the banks, but if there are I am inclined to think these savings must be in a minority of accounts. I say that because credit buying in Canada has now reached an all-time high. If saving deposits in the banks were as large as some might assume, then credit buying would become less and less all the time. Instead of

National Housing Act
that it is constantly growing, and the bill itself in a sense is an accentuation of that very situation, although I am not criticizing the bill on that account because in the final analysis it is a choice of whether one wants to pay rent or put some money into what will in time become an asset.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to reach an anticlimax in the last few minutes at my disposal, and I will therefore conclude this part of my speech by saying once again that this bill to my mind is purely a financial rather than a housing measure. It is a purely financial measure designed to perpetuate the government's present inflationary policy.
The other points I want to make are in respect of administration. I believe it is time notice was taken of certain matters of administration under this bill. I believe any contractor or anyone who undertakes to build a house for a client should be bonded in some way or other so the borrower or the person building a home will not lose his money. I am not blaming the government for this, nor is it the fault of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, but something has gone wrong in the initial administration in regard to some of these loans.
I wish to bring one case in particular to the attention of hon. members. I want to make it public not because I am blaming the minister but because other people should know what is liable to happen. I have a case here where a gentleman wanted to build a home. He got in touch with a contractor, evidently through a real estate firm, and he applied for a loan. He made a deposit of $1,330 with either the real estate firm or the contractor, I am not too clear which; but in any event either the contractor or the real estate firm in the meantime went broke and the result was that this prospective home owner lost his $1,330. I took the case up with the minister and he was good enough to look into it and inform me of the exact situation. I am sure the minister will not mind if I read his explanation into the record. This concerns the case of Mr. W. L. Blackburn and his National Housing Act loan application. This gentleman resides at Pincher Creek, Alberta. The minister's explanation was as follows:
Mr. Blackburn's loan application (without any deposit) was filed with the Lethbridge branch of the corporation by a local real estate firm. It was not necessary to deposit any money with the application. On June 5 that office wrote to Mr. Blackburn and informed him that his application had been declined. The deposit was never under the control of Central Mortgage, nor was the real estate firm authorized to act on behalf of the corporation.
[Mr. Hansell.l
I am very sorry that Mr. Blackburn has not been successful in having his deposit refunded and can only suggest that he consult a solicitor forthwith.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that some steps should be taken to protect a person in that situation. There must be hundreds of people who do not know exactly what the initial procedure is in regard to these things. I believe every contractor and real estate firm that has anything whatsoever to do with the National Housing Act should be bonded so that when a person undertakes a loan he will not lose any money under the bill.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have another couple of things I wanted to suggest but I see your keen eye on me and on the clock, so I had better stop. When this bill goes to committee I will perhaps ask the minister some questions along the lines 1 have indicated, and which I still wish to pursue. Let me conclude by emphasizing that I believe this bill is designed to perpetuate the present financial policy of the government.

Mr. Speaker, in the early stages of these debates, particularly, I have frequently heard members say they had looked over the new bill and received it more in sorrow than in anger. I am sorry I cannot make that statement today. As a matter of fact, as I look at the bill it provokes in me feelings both of sorrow and of anger. Surely the test of any housing bill must be this. Is it going to provide more housing for the people of the

National Housing Act
country than is provided by the legislation which it replaces? On that test I do not think there is any question but that this bill will be an utter failure and that it will not supply materially more housing than has been supplied by the legislation we have on the statute books at the present time.
The scheme which the bill contains has had a good deal of publicity which has led a large number of people to think it will be easier for them to obtain housing. In other words it has given rise to a great many hopes. I am very much afraid that the hopes of most of these people are not going to be realized. I cannot see where this particular legislation is going to make it possible for many more people to secure housing than were able to secure it under the old act.
On the face of it, of course, the lowering of the down payment to 10 per cent, or the so-called lowering of it, and the increase in the amortization period to 25 years, would make it appear that a great many more people would be able to take advantage of the provisions of the National Housing Act than have been able to do so up to date. This was certainly the idea which I myself secured when the legislation was announced. Whilst I was home over the holidays a considerable number of people expressed this opinion to me, and also expressed the hope that under this new legislation they would at last be able to secure a home.
An examination of this legislation, however, as it is likely to work out in practice, has convinced me at least that a very small number of people who were not in position to take advantage of the old act will be benefited. In other words, I am sorry to say, I have to come to the conclusion that the bill is, in the words of a parliamentarian of the last century, "a delusion, a mockery and a snare."

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
What the government is doing in this bill, Mr. Speaker, is playing what they no doubt think is smart politics. They tell the people they have given them a 10 per cent down payment house, which sounds very attractive. It is something about which a large number of people have been talking for a long time. However, the catch is that this house has to be built for $8,000, and it has to be built to the standards set by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The government knows just as well as anyone in this chamber that a house of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation standards cannot be built for $8,000, in most

parts of this country at least. Thus, in effect, there is no such thing as a 10 per cent down payment.
As has been pointed out by several speakers already, on what most of us would consider to be the minimum priced house which could be built, that is $10,000, the down payment is going to be $1,400 or 14 per cent. A house costing probably closer to the average, we will say $12,000, will require a down payment of $2,000 or 16-6 per cent. In other words, there is no such thing as a 10 per cent down payment. It is a misnomer, a snare and a delusion. Whether or not it has been done by design, this bill has certainly roused false hopes in the minds of a large number of people.
I know the government defenders of this bill will say that the down payment has been considerably reduced, that on a $10,000 house it has been reduced from $2,000 to $1,400. Many more people, it is said, will then be able to buy a house because of this reduced down payment. Undoubtedly some people will benefit. A certain number of people who could not raise $2,000 will be able to raise $1,400. However, not nearly as many people will be benefited as one would imagine.
Over the Christmas recess I talked to a number of builders in Calgary, who told me that as many as 70 per cent of the people who had built houses during the past year with a $2,000 down payment had borrowed between $500 and $1,000 in order to meet that down payment. These people had gone to their relatives, friends or other sources and borrowed this money in order to get the down payment. It would seem, therefore, that a considerable number of people having less than $2,000, but having $1,400, have already been taken care of. The number who will be able to benefit by this reduction in the down payment is much less than one might otherwise expect.
The chief reason, however, that not so many people will be able to benefit from the bill is that the number who will be able to meet the monthly payment required is not greatly increased. The change in the monthly payment is more or less infinitesimal. As an example, on a $10,000 house there will be a mortgage of $8,600. If we assume that is going to be at 5 [DOT] 5 per cent interest, which has been rather a common assumption here although the minister said it would be between 5 and 6 per cent, the monthly payment required to amortize this over 25 years comes to $52.50. I believe this afternoon the minister said,

when some such figure was quoted, that it was $52.45. The five cents is not very material.
Under the existing scheme, on a $10,000 house where a $2,000 down payment has been made, with an $8,000 mortgage amortized over 20 years at 5-25 per cent, the monthly payment is $53.66. In other words there is a difference of only $1.16 per month or $13.92 per year. That is all the man buying a minimum priced house at $10,000 will save. This means that only a small number of people who were not able to buy a house before because their monthly salary was not sufficient will now be able to do so. As a matter of fact, I would think that with the other factors to be considered there would be no difference whatever.
During this debate it has been assumed, and the minister has never said anything to the contrary, that one of the rules which will continue in effect will be that 23 per cent of income is the maximum which may be paid for housing. So far as a $10,000 house is concerned, we must add to the payment of $52.50 for amortization the amounts for taxes and fire insurance. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) put certain figures for taxes and fire insurance on the record this afternoon. In his calculations he arrived at a yearly income of $3,860, and the minister has not disputed that. I allowed a much smaller amount for taxes and fire insurance, $16 per month.
