speechtext:
I think I should make it
clear, as I attempted to do this afternoon, that the figure of $3,860 is the figure one arrives at assuming a lending value of $12,000. Of course if the lending value is more or less than that a corresponding figure will be determined by that same formula.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am assuming a $10,000
house with a mortgage of $8,600, and calculating that we still get this figure of $52.50 a month, you add another $16 for taxes and insurance. I am sure the minister will say that is the absolute minimum for taxes and insurance. There are very few places where you could get them for that. The total monthly payment required is then $68.50. This should work out as being 23 per cent of $297.80, or nearly $300.00 per month, a yearly income of $3,600. Now, that is the income required to purchase -a minimum priced house. No one with an income below approximately $3,600 is going to derive any advantage from this bill. I believe that has been pointed out.
The unfortunate fact is that the majority of the citizens of this country have incomes
National Housing Act
lower than $3,600. This housing bill is not for them at all. This measure has not been designed for the lower income groups in this country. I do not know that we should even speak of them as the lower income group. It has not been designed for at least two-thirds of the citizens in this country. Surely a housing scheme which is designed for the people in the upper one-third of the income brackets of this country could hardly be fairly called a national housing scheme.
Another matter which has received a considerable amount of criticism and in respect of which the bill can be criticized is the interest rate. It has been indicated to us that an interest rate of 5i or 6 per cent is what we are likely to have in connection with this housing scheme, and that this rate is to be allowed on what would amount to guaranteed loans. I realize the guarantee is not to the extent of 100 per cent, but it gets pretty close to that. For all practical purposes, these are guaranteed loans. It does not seem to me that a rate of 5J or 6 per cent is justified on loans of this kind.
There has been a good deal of talk about whether it will be possible to get sufficient money from lending institutions, including the banks, to finance the building we would all like to see. I do not wish to discuss that phase of the matter at the moment, but it seems to me that with a guaranteed loan there should be a possibility of getting the money at interest rates lower than 5i or 6 per cent. Certainly I do not know where money could be invested, with practically no risk, at anything like those rates of interest. Rates of that kind are being secured where there is a considerable amount of risk.
To sum up this phase of the matter 1 would say that this whole thing looks very much like one of those schemes where the government is promising a great deal, where it is doing a lot of talking about the benefits which will be secured by Canadians from this legislation, but where actually it is handing to the Canadian people a fully inflated paper bag containing practically nothing.
What the public should understand in connection with this bill-and, so far as I have been able to determine, what it does not understand-is that there are several things which make it much less attractive than it has thus far been represented. First of all, I have found that a great many people have not gone ahead to secure housing because they are waiting for this scheme to come into operation. They have been thinking that they would secure houses more easily and cheaply under this scheme than was possible before. One thing the general public should

National Housing Act
understand is that houses under this scheme will not be available for some time. I have heard from builders that it will be at least five or six months.
Then, on the average, the down payment is not much less than it was under the old scheme. On what one might call an average house costing $11,000 the down payment is only about $250 less than it was under the old scheme, and that is not a very material difference. Certainly it will not enable many more people to take advantage of housing legislation.
The third point is that the end cost of houses under this scheme is going to be considerably higher, and this is inevitable due to the 5J per cent interest rate and the longer period of amortization.
The fourth point the general public should understand before it gives or withholds approval is that the new plan is not designed for the lower income groups. It will do them no good whatsoever.
I suggest that nothing the minister and members supporting the government have said in connection with this housing bill comes to grips with the realities of the housing situation in Canada. As I have said, the great majority of our population cannot secure homes under this or any other plan, because their incomes are too low. What does the government envisage for the majority of the people in this country in the matter of housing? It is quite evident, I suggest, that the government has no plans for them. Those people are going to be left to their own devices, and without housing. So far as the government is concerned that is all there is to it.
A housing scheme in this country should produce houses that the majority of people in the lower income groups could secure. I suggest that is by no means impossible. We have heard a considerable amount of talk about subsidized housing from members in the C.C.F. I do not think it is necessary to go into subsidized housing in order to secure homes for the middle and lower income groups. There are two ways in which cheaper houses can be produced. The first is by improved efficiency in the building of the houses, and the lowering of costs. This involves a considerable number of factors, including prefabricated houses and utilizing other building techniques. It also involves more efficient work on the part of contractors and carpenters, plumbers, bricklayers and other tradesmen who are connected with the building of houses. I do not think many people will believe, for example, that it is not possible to lay more bricks per hour or to put
[Mr. Harkness.l
on more square feet of plaster per hour than has been done or is being done, on the average, in the building of houses today.
More efficient building methods and the utilization of new techniques can reduce building costs quite considerably. I suggest, too, that houses can be built at a lower cost for the lower income groups by lowering the present standards set by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. No one maintains that everybody has to have a suit of clothes worth $100 or an automobile worth $3,000. Similarly, I do not see why it should be considered that everybody should have, let us say, a $10,000 or a $12,000 house.
It is quite possible to build smaller houses than are required by present standards. They can be built without many of the costly features and at much less money. I know this is so because in Alberta we have several examples. A number of attractive small houses have been built at Devon, an area that I know is familiar to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham). I think he will agree that they are attractive. They have been sold for as low as $5,500 to the present occupants. They are not slums or shacks. Many of them are attractive, and they are well built. A few more houses of somewhat similar design have been built just west of Calgary, at Cochrane, as part of the power development.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. member recommend these as family houses?

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, I certainly would. A large number of those houses, at any rate, are quite satisfactory for small families, and would be available at a cost which people could afford. Thousands upon thousands would be able to get out of basement suites and one-room flats, thus getting away from the very bad living conditions they have to suffer.
During the last summer I did a considerable amount of canvassing, and I was horrified by the living conditions I found right in the city of Calgary. Numbers of people were hived up in little shacks. There are in that city even now a considerable number of what we used to call homesteader shacks. They came as a sort of package deal from the T. Eaton Company and various lumber companies. They have slanting roofs and are built like chicken coops. I had not seen any of them on the prairies; they disappeared from the farms years ago. But they are still there right in the city of Calgary, and fair-sized families are living in them. Certainly houses such as have been built at Devon and various other places in Alberta are so much superior and

so much better that I do not think anybody would dispute that people would be much better off living in houses of that sort.
As a matter of fact I think one of the chief reasons so many in the lower income groups cannot secure housing is the standards set by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and by municipal authorities. It seems to me that a great deal of the lack and need of housing could be met at the present time by setting aside an area just beyond where present building is taking place-I mean outside of a city-and applying to it much lower building restrictions than exist at the present time in the cities of Canada.
I see nothing in the world wrong, for example, with a house that has 750 or 800 square feet rather than the 1,150 or 1,200 required by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I see nothing whatever wrong with building houses with softwood floors, fir floors rather than hardwood floors, and there are various other things along the same lines. If that is done, and it can be done quite readily, houses can be built, as they actually have been built in Alberta, for prices ranging from $5,500 up to $7,500, houses which would be quite satisfactory to a large number of people and which they would be delighted to get.
Another matter that has arisen during the debate and about which quite a bit has been said is the shortage of serviced land.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: I did not want to interrupt the hon. member while he was in the middle of a particular theme, but I should like to say to him now that the houses at Devon which he commended so highly were all financed under the National Housing Act.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am very glad to hear it. I did not know how they were financed, but I spoke to one of the contractors who built some of them and he told me they had sold at prices ranging from $5,500 to $7,500. I have never since been able to see any reason why the same thing could not be done on the outskirts of Edmonton, Calgary, Toronto, or any city that you wish to mention.
I had started to say something about serviced land. I think one of the chief reasons there is so little serviced land is that everybody is trying to build in a few places in or immediately adjacent to large cities. This matter is tied up with the decentralization of industry. There have been many speeches in the house urging the government to take what steps it could to bring about the decentralization of industry, but unfortunately very little has been done. As a
National Housing Act
result more and more people are rushing to Toronto, Montreal and such areas, bringing about a terrific shortage of serviced land.
There are plenty of communities throughout Canada where serviced land would not be difficult to obtain. There are plenty of communities where the people already there would be delighted to see more building, in the smaller cities and towns. I think that part of the problem could be met very readily by encouraging loans in such areas, but those are the very areas where it is difficult for people to get loans. In the smaller places it is much more difficult in most cases to get C.M.H.C. financing than in places like Toronto, Montreal, Calgary, Edmonton or Vancouver.
Perhaps I have given the impression that I think very little of the bill, and that is the case. The only reason I will vote for it is that it will help a very limited number of people, and in view of the fact that it will help a limited number of people I cannot see my way clear to vote against it. But certainly the number of people it will help is so limited that I think the government should allow the bill to be amended when it is before the banking and commerce committee in such a way that it will become of some real value.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I listened with interest to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) refer to the tarpaper shacks in his riding. Tonight we heard the member for the adjacent riding of Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode) more or less denying it but apologizing for the condition. Neither of these members needs to worry at all, because you will find tarpaper shacks in every riding in this dominion. As a matter of fact I venture to say that more tarpaper shacks were built last year than all the units under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. They continue to be built for the simple reason that while these people are not anxious to live in these shacks, they cannot meet the requirements of this bill or any government legislation that has ever existed so far as the securing of a home is concerned.
These are the people who need homes; therefore I am going to say a few words on their behalf. I do not intend to deal with the particular bill before us, a bill that I call one for the upper ten. It does not have anything to do with the group to whom I am going to refer. Hansard will disclose that several excellent speeches have been made contributing, to my mind, very valuable information which if made use of would help solve the housing problem. That applies to members of every party who have spoken.

National Housing Act
The housing problem is a growing one, and during the last tew years we have not even held our own with the housing demand. I am not blaming the government entirely. I am blaming what is commonly called free or private enterprise even more, for it has failed us. For instance, insurance companies entered the housing field when they had no other outlet for their funds. They took things over lock, stock and barrel for the purpose of investment, not as a scheme to supply homes for the people of Canada. When other more lucrative fields opened up they withdrew from the scene, and the banks will do the same thing in a few years' time.
The free or private enterprise group of builders in this country have practically left the speculative field of building entirely alone, and they are not interested in coming back to it. Neither the government nor private enterprise have given a thought to the millions of Canadians whose earnings are below the $3,600 or $3,700 mark. We in this group are particularly worried about these people, and we are not alone. There are many Liberal, Conservative and Social Credit members who are just as alarmed that nothing is being done for these people.
It may well be that after the next election several of the present members will not return to the house. They may fail at the polls or they may not be chosen. What is going to be their lot? Many of them will be entitled to the maximum pension of $3,000 a year, and after living in Ottawa for so long they will need homes. Under this scheme they will come to the government for a home under this act but every one of them will be turned down. I feel that the lending provisions should be broadened to take account of character, because I fail to see why any former member with a steady income of $3,000 who applies for a loan should be turned down. I think his character should be sufficient recompense for the lack of the $700 needed to make up the necessary income.
I have taken certain figures from the 1951 census. I find that we have 5| million wage earners in Canada, 4 million of whom earn less than $3,000 a year, and one out of three less than $2,000 a year. Furthermore I find that in the large cities 32 per cent of all workers, married and single, earn less than $1,500 a year. Ottawa, for instance, has 24 per cent of its wage-earning heads of families receiving less than $2,000 a year. This bill does not mean a thing to them. Its language is not understood by them, and the intention of the bill is not to cover them.
Yet I feel that if any particular group needs assistance it is the group with incomes of less than $3,500 a year. It is this group that needs homes. Other people can find other means to raise money to build their own homes, through the loan companies or banks, and they would do so if this scheme were not in effect. These people are the victims of economic conditions, quite often beyond their control. I will admit that sometimes it is their own fault, but generally speaking they are the victims of our present system. But they too are human; they too have feelings; they too have families; they too have children they would like to have properly housed. They would like decent homes in which to live just the same as the person getting $5,000 or $10,000 a year. That aspect has not been considered at all.
Bearing that in mind, I would suggest to the minister that after this bill is put through, as I presume it will be, he set up a commission to investigate ways and means of providing homes for this type of person who is industrious, who has a sound moral character, who is a good Canadian citizen, who was probably born in this country and who has prospects of raising a fine family. All he wants is some assistance in order to build a home.
The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) made some reference to rural areas when he spoke. I feel the same as he does. Something should be done for the people in the rural areas who also need decent homes. All you need do is go by train or drive a car across this country, and in every province you will find evidence that what I say is absolutely true. A vast number of poorly-built houses, unpainted, sometimes covered with tarpaper, are to be found. To me they constitute a visible disgrace to a wealthy country like Canada.
Having concentrated on the urban areas, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have neglected entirely this worth-while field. If the people in our rural areas were properly housed it would help to attract tourists to different points throughout the country where they could look at decent homes and see our citizens living under decent conditions. But today you see houses with holes in the roof, barns that are propped up in order to keep them from falling completely over. That kind of thing is not a credit to this wealthy country.
This bill will not change that at all. I am going to suggest that in addition to making a survey in connection with the low income group the minister also make a survey of the

rural areas. As someone said, it is a good idea to have the people scattered instead of congested in possible slum areas. Under the old scheme the insurance companies and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation were not interested very much in the rural areas because the lack of fire protection and other facilities made their investment less safe than investment in organized centres.
But I would point out that even though there may be a lack of such facilities in the rural areas, they would find a higher moral responsibility among the people. Those people would be more likely to look after the loan they had acquired in order to build a home. They would meet their obligations on a higher moral basis than the people in organized centres. I realize I am sticking out my neck, but it is my impression that people in the country have a high standard of morality. This would compensate for the lack of firefighting equipment and other things. If we are going to assist these people it is essential that money be made available at not more than 2 per cent. Other speakers have dealt with this so I shall not go into any further detail.
I am almost sure it was the last Liberal government of British Columbia that paid particular attention to housing in rural areas. They reduced taxation on farm homes to a nominal amount in order to encourage the painting and improvement and enlargement of homes, as well as installing facilities such as baths and toilets inside the houses. Over the last few years those concessions have resulted in a definite improvement in the homes being built and those already built. That is quite evident as you cross the province of British Columbia today.
I suggest to the minister that he instruct the banks to be particularly helpful to the borrowers in rural areas, to reverse the treatment that these people have received during the last year or two from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after looking at this bill I have the impression that I have looked at Aladdin's lamp, because it seems to me it contains magic. Some people look at the bill and say, "The banks will be taking over the mortgage business." Other people look at the bill and say, "The government is going out of the mortgage business." This afternoon 1 heard hon. members describe the bankers as profiteers, while others described the bankers as the men who would be dragged up and forced to tell the poor man
National Housing Act
who could not pay his mortgage money that foreclosure was his lot. Whom are we to believe?
I believe sincerely that we have a middle of the road bill. If the Canadian public were in the galleries tonight I think they would know why they had elected the Liberal party to power. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) and the government have paved the way for constructive suggestions. I do not think everything that has been said by the opposition is wrong, but on the other hand I do not think everything contained in the bill is wrong. After all, we are lawmakers and we should use common sense. To me this bill is common sense.
I understand that this bill is going to give the banks greater powers, as has been stated by some hon. members. As I have said, other hon. members have stated that these powers would be centralized in the government's hands. The reality is that the government is going to guarantee the loans and in effect will use the offices of the banks and their available liquid assets in order to make those loans. Many hon. members are businessmen and they know what it costs in the way of upkeep, etc., to run an office. I am sure that before this bill was drafted the government conferred with the banks and came to some agreement under which they would use their facilities so there would be more offices and more available assets from which to serve the Canadian people in a more efficient way.
As I said a while ago, the Minister of Public Works in bringing this legislation forward has paved the way for suggestions. As the bill is going to go to the banking and commerce committee I consider it my privilege to make a few suggestions to the government. I am sure they will be welcomed, because this is not a hush-hush bill, nor is it a camouflaged bill. The minister placed the bill before the house on December 16, just before the recess, in order that hon. members would be aware that it would be discussed after the recess. In doing so I think the government deserves to be congratulated, for it provided hon. members with an opportunity to examine the legislation presently under discussion.
Under the old act, wherever lending institutions were granting loans Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would not compete with private enterprise. This procedure had a somewhat harmful effect in certain regions. I cannot speak for all of Canada but I can speak for my own constituency of Longueuil. About 20 per cent of the population of the

National Housing Act
constituency of Longueuil benefited under the old act, and I believe that under the present bill more people will be able to benefit by Central Mortgage and Housing loans. Under the old act the lending institutions were providing 75 per cent of the amount of a loan while the government was supplying the remaining 25 per cent. "The man who pays the piper calls the tune"; therefore the lending institutions chose the regions in which they would operate and that is one of the reasons why approximately 80 per cent of my constituents did not benefit by C.M.H.C. joint loans under the old act. This new bill alters that situation and the Canadian people now are guaranteeing the loans.
It is true we are using the banks in making these loans, but the banks in each region are well aware of people's needs. They are in daily contact with the population, with business people and ordinary individuals. They know the people and they know their credit needs. It should also be borne in mind that the government is now guaranteeing these loans and therefore should be permitted to "call the tune".
I believe this is a well balanced bill. On the one hand we have the government guaranteeing the loans and on the other hand we have the services of the banks. The banks are not merely profiteers in this regard. After all they are giving service. They supply their offices, staff, and their liquid assets-we must remember that.
I believe that this bill, once it incorporates certain suggestions made by some hon. members, will be a good bill and the Canadian people will benefit by it. I do not think it is the desire of the Canadian people that they be given homes. If that were the case they would have elected a socialist government. The Liberal party and this government are striving to look after the welfare of the Canadian people and this bill in my estimation will, when enacted, become a welfare act.
Some hon. members have discussed the possibility of building better and more attractive homes. I agree with that. I believe we must strive to improve the architectural design of the Canadian home. A man is judged by the way he talks and a country is judged largely by its habitat. In other words, people coming into Canada will judge Canadians by the outward appearance of their homes. I would suggest that the government give further consideration to this matter and encourage architects in Canada to design better and more attractive modern homes.
[Mr. Vincent 1
I want to draw the attention of the government to one other point. On December 16, 1953, the Minister of Public Works stated, as reported at page 998 of Hansard:
In addition, it is proposed to reduce the down payment from the 20 per cent now required under the National Housing Act. The amount of the loans will be 90 per cent of the first $8,000 and 70 per cent of the balance of the lending value," . . .
There is one suggestion I would like to make on this point. Would it not be possible to have the loan made in direct proportion instead of having it made in inverse proportion, because I think families who have three, four or five children would like to benefit from the long-term loan provisions of this bill. Canadians should be given the same advantage whether they require a $12,000 or $8,000 home. If the government would consider that I think it would be much appreciated by the Canadian people.
There is one other aspect I would like to touch on, and it concerns the federal-provincial scheme. I sincerely regret that the province of Quebec has not seen fit to accept the benefits of the National Housing Act. I would say it is one of the reasons we have such chaotic housing conditions in the vicinity of Montreal. In the city of Jacques Cartier we have about 30,000 people living without sewers and without the benefit of a water system. Under this act the provincial government could have assisted those people.
I would ask the government and the Minister of Public Works whether it would not be possible to approach the authorities in the province of Quebec and discuss this matter with them. By bringing this matter to their attention in a fair and frank manner the government might be able to persuade the authorities in the province of Quebec to accept the benefits of this section of the act. An agreement along these lines would relieve one of the greatest housing problems which exist in the region of Montreal. Conditions there have to be seen to be believed. I am not blaming any officials or any governments, but I would seriously urge the government to consider bringing this matter to the attention of the Quebec authorities and attempting to arrive at some arrangement whereby this area may be relieved of its housing problem.
In closing I wish to thank hon. members for having listened to me in this speech. I sincerely hope that all those concerned with the good of Canada will do their utmost- especially those who are members of the banking and commerce committee-to look into this bill and I hope that if any changes have to be made, they will be made constructively, for the benefit of all Canadians.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
first of all I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Vincent), who has just taken his seat, on the excellent speech he made. It is the first time I have heard him speak in the house, and I think perhaps it is his first speech, he being a new member. If it is, he certainly deserves great credit.
The subject we are discussing tonight is, of course, one in which we are all greatly interested, although perhaps the interest is not the same in all parts of Canada. As a matter of fact I greatly doubt whether the housing act affects us in the maritimes as much as it affects the people in Ontario or in Quebec in and around Montreal. It certainly does not affect us particularly in my own constituency, which is a rural one in which about 80 per cent of the people are interested in farming.
In our part of the country we have some vacant houses which we should be glad to have filled up by people coming in. As a matter of fact, last August when I was going through my constituency I visited a part of it in which there were a great many vacant houses, in fact over a thousand of them. It was rather sad to see so many vacant houses. At that time I thought that if only those houses were in some other part of Canada in which there is a scarcity of housing, what a great benefit it would be to some people. I am, of course, referring to the Gagetown camp training area which was taken over by the government a year ago.
It has been interesting to hear the prices mentioned for the construction of houses in this country. The thought came to me that on some of these farms there is a large house, a large barn and other buildings, but I doubt very much whether the farmer, for all his possessions-including house, land and so on-received $10,000. It seems that $10,000 is a great deal of money to pay for the building of a small house. I realize, of course, that this is a result of economic conditions, the scarcity of supplies with which to build houses, perhaps the great cost of the labour put into the house, and the high cost of serviced land on which it was built.
I am like everyone else in the house here. We are all interested in seeing that the people are properly housed. I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that it does not make any difference whether we are Liberal, Conservative, Social Credit or C.C.F.; we all have the same interest, namely that we want to see the people of this country properly housed. I know it makes no difference whether we
National Housing Act
live in the maritimes or in the west or what the economic situation is; we all have the same idea.
This Bill No. 102, which was explained by the minister the other day, as he told us is being substituted for the existing National Housing Act. Under that act many houses were built. I think the minister told us that some 80,000 houses were built last year. That is a large number of houses. We have heard the shortage of houses in Canada estimated by some at 200,000 and by others at 500,000. I do not think anyone really knows what the shortage of houses in Canada is today.
What this bill will do to overcome this great shortage we can only conjecture at the present time. I have my own ideas on the matter; other hon. members have theirs. It is difficult for us to say at this time just what the result will be. We will not know that result until the legislation has been in force and the activities under it have been tried out. Then only shall we be able to say what the result will be.
We expected great things of the National Housing Act. I remember when the debate took place in this house a few years ago. At that time we thought the National Housing Act was going to solve the housing problem here in the Dominion of Canada. Unfortunately it has not done so, and for that fact many reasons have been given. I have already mentioned some. We now understand that the great difficulty is the lack of money.
As I say, the object of this new bill is to build houses. This government bill proposes three things in order to carry out that purpose. The first is to reduce the down payment on a house to 10 per cent of the value and to extend the time for repayment to 25 or 30 years. We have had a great deal of comment upon this proposal. The second proposal is to put the chartered banks into the mortgage business and to have Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation insure the mortgages in order to protect the banks from loss. The premiums on this insurance are to be paid by the borrowers. The third proposal is to authorize the Bank of Canada to provide the chartered banks with cash on the security of the insured mortgages they hold.
As I said, under the National Housing Act there seemed to be no trouble raising money through the insurance companies. We were told by the minister a few days ago, I think, that the insurance companies sold government bonds to the extent of $800 million and also to the extent of $200 million more, making $1 billion that they invested in housing in

National Housing Act
this country. Of course it is the people's money which had been paid in to the insurance companies by way of premiums, but it was paid in over a long period of years. Insurance is something that you take out for 20 years or for life. It was not money that was payable on demand, and naturally the insurance companies could invest this money without feeling that those who had paid their premiums would be affected in any way.
Under this bill the money is to be obtained from the banks. Money is placed in banks, of course, under short-term arrangements, and it represents the savings of the Canadian people. The minister has told us that we shall have to change the Bank Act so it will provide for long-term investment instead of short-term lending. This is something which may not be regarded too lightly by the Canadian people. During the last few days we have heard many arguments to the effect that this proposal is not good as far as the investments of the people are concerned. The bank's first duty, of course, is to protect the savings of the depositors. The money is there to be called for at any time.
This afternoon the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) gave us an interesting lecture on the banking system. He said he was sure that certain members were not stupid, but certain statements they made to the effect that the money in the banks or lent by the banks was the depositors' money were altogether wrong. Well, I listened to the hon. member's lecture this afternoon, and I expect he will think I am stupid because I am afraid I did not derive very much benefit from it.
I am not an authority on the banking system of this country, but I do know that if a bank had no deposits-well of course that would be too ridiculous to consider, because you would not have a bank at all. It is certainly true that the smaller the bank and the fewer the deposits, the less lending that bank can do. The more deposits a bank has, of course, the more lending the bank can do and the better position it is in. As I say the deposits must, in some way, have something to do with the lending which a bank is in a position to do.
So far as the protection of the banks is concerned, the bill provides that mortgages will be given. The mortgages will protect the bank to a certain extent, and in that way the depositors will be protected also. It is true that the bill realizes that money must be deposited before it is made available, and provision has been made that will enable the banks to take the insured mortgages they
(Mr. Brooks.]
hold to the Bank of Canada and get cash for them. This will not be the same kind of cash the depositors had earned and put into the banks for safekeeping. It will be cash fresh from the printing press. It will have cost the bank nothing, and will have no value except what it can absorb from the money which the people have earned and with which it will circulate.
The net upshot of the whole proceeding may be that the earned money which the people entrusted to the banks for safekeeping will have been removed and inflationary money which cost the bank nothing put in its place. This inflationary money will absorb value from the true money with which it will circulate, and everybody will find that his money has lost some of its value, though few will know how it happened.
The matter of mortgages has also been mentioned by a number of speakers. As was pointed out, the onus of foreclosing the mortgage will be placed upon the banks. Neither the government nor the government agencies will be in the position of having to carry this unpopular burden. The banks will have to bear it. I do not know what the number of foreclosures is likely to be. That is something which will be revealed in the future. I know that even people who have borrowed anything from one-half to two-thirds of the money to build a house have had to default, for different reasons, and the mortgage has been foreclosed. I am satisfied that with the granting of hundreds of thousands of mortgages there will be many which will have to be foreclosed.
I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that there are many reasons for the shortage of houses in Canada. The minister mentioned some the other day. People come to this country from other countries, and naturally in a cold country like Canada they need a place in which to live. Then there is the natural increase of population in this country. In addition there are other reasons. First, we have noticed that there is a movement of population from the rural areas to the towns and villages in every section of Canada. For instance, the older people used to live on the farms with their sons and daughters. Now they move into the villages and towns and take up small houses. Due to the great increase in mechanization of the farms, one or two men can run a farm which used to need three or four.
Another reason for the increased need for houses is the movement from one province to another. I can speak with knowledge of

that because I know that from the three maritime provinces-perhaps I might say four without offending my good friends from N ewf oundland-

speechtext: The Atlantic provinces.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
We are all Atlantic provinces but there are three maritime provinces. There has been a continued exodus of people to the central part of Canada, to the large industrial centres such as Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton and other places. This has caused great congestion in these parts of Canada. It has also left vacant houses in the sections of the country from which those people came. I know young people have left my constituency to go to Toronto, and have left fairly good houses which have had to be sold at low prices. These houses would accommodate families with three, four or five children. The people have gone to Toronto or Montreal. When they return for a visit they tell you they live in one room or two rooms. It is impossible to find accommodation in the big cities.
I recall that last fall I was going through Montreal, and I met a young man whom I knew in the park in front of the Windsor hotel. He had his wife and three children with him. I asked him how he was getting along and he said that he was getting good wages but had no place to live. They were living in two rooms in a basement, and he said the only comfort they had was when they could take the children out to sit in the park.
This situation has developed in Canada as a result of our economic situation. I was pleased indeed to hear the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) suggest a solution. I think it is a solution which is linked up with the housing problem in Canada, and that is the decentralization of industry. We can accommodate two or three times the population we have in the mari-times, and we would have two or three times our population if we could retain our young people there and give them employment. I have often pressed for this in the House of Commons, and I believe we will always have an acute housing situation in Canada until there is some decentralization of industry in this country.
As the hon. member said, around Toronto and Montreal one of the great reasons housing costs so much is that you cannot get serviced land, with sewers and water and other things required for good housing. In the smaller towns and cities of the maritime provinces I am satisfied that you could get
National Housing Act
serviced land, and better land, for a third or a quarter of the cost up here in the larger centres.
I am not going to deal with this question at greater length. Of course if hon. members wanted to criticize they would say, "But you have not the facilities in the maritime provinces, especially in New Brunswick, to entice industry.'' This is very true. We want cheap electrical power in New Brunswick. That province has great possibilities so far as industrial development is concerned, but today we are being held back because we have not cheap electrical power, and our financial position does not merit our going into it too extensively, although the province is anxious to do so.
This is one way in which the federal government could assist the different provinces needing help. It could assist in the decentralization of industry and, in that way, relieve the housing problem. The problem is not a temporary one; it has existed since the last war, and even before that. And I am satisfied that as long as the present economic condition exists we will have these housing conditions.
I would hope that the regulations in connection with the building of houses would not be too strict. As member after member has pointed out, a man who has to earn his living by daily toil will not be in a position to buy or to build $8,000 or $10,000 houses. It is almost impossible for the working man today to build a house costing that much.
I recall that under the Veterans Land Act provision was made whereby veterans could build their own houses. Those houses were built under the supervision of the Department of Veterans Affairs. Over 10,000 of them were built by veterans in Canada, with the assistance of their friends and neighbours, bringing about a saving of about $2,000 on each house. There are thousands of men across Canada who would like to build their own homes and who, if given the opportunity, would do so. I hope the regulations will not be too strict and that every encouragement will be given prospective home owners for the construction of their own homes.
I do not think I have anything further to add. This bill will not help in any way the matter of slum clearance in our larger cities. I know of cities in which houses have been standing for a good many years. Due to the ravages of time and the fact that rentals paid have not permitted improvements, many of those houses today are in such a condition that they should be condemned. One can find this in practically every city in Canada.

speechtext:
The minister says the bill
would help. I am thinking of a city I know better than any other, and I shall not mention it by name. The wooden houses in that city were built many years ago, and there are three or four tenants in each house. One will find whole streets of houses of that kind. Many years ago there was a fire in that city and it had to be rebuilt in a hurry. As the years have gone by the houses have become dilapidated. I doubt very much whether this bill would be of any benefit. The cost would be too great, and many other difficulties would face the builders.
I am not opposed to the bill; I do not intend to vote against it. I am one who wishes it every success, because a housing bill which will provide homes for our people is badly needed in this country. I hope this bill is the answer, but I cannot help feeling that it has many weaknesses.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, ten minutes to ten o'clock on a Friday evening is not the most desirable time to make a speech in the House of Commons. I do not know, sir, whether you would wish me to call it ten o'clock.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Get a start, anyway.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I want to be kind to the minister. I would not like to see the debate on such an important subject collapse at this moment, so that he would be called upon to wind up the debate when he is in an exhausted state, after having listened so patiently to the words of wisdom from this side of the house.
There can be no question about the importance of the bill before us. On its title page we find this; "An act to promote the construction of new houses, the repair and modernization of existing houses, and the improvement of housing and living conditions"-a very worthy objective indeed. Then the bill is divided into a series of parts. Part I is headed, "Insurance mortgage loans"; part II bears the heading, "Housing for rental purposes and land assembly", and part III, "Housing redevelopment", and so on.
In the last two days the attention of the house has been directed to part I, the new section. Most of the points in respect of that part have been covered most effectively by those who have preceded me in the debate. Consequently it is not my intention to indulge in any repetition with regard to these matters. I noticed that in his opening remarks yesterday the minister, with becoming modesty, said he and all of us, for that


matter, are not complacent with regard to the housing situation in Canada. And he said that with good reason. There is no ground to be complacent about housing conditions in Canada.
The government has been in the housing business now for almost 20 years. As was pointed out yesterday, the Dominion Housing Act was passed in 1935 and then was superseded in 1944 by the National Housing Act, the latter act of course being the legislation we have before us now with modifications. What has happened during the 20 years? I think no scientific basis has been established for us to estimate the housing requirements of the nation. At page 1313 of Hansard for yesterday the minister said:
The number of new housing units built In any one year must be related not only to our need for housing, but also to the effective demand by the Canadian people for housing.
I ran across the phrase "effective demand" eight years ago when I first began to investigate housing conditions in the city of Winnipeg. It is a very tricky phrase indeed. I do not know what its interpretation is, but I discovered when I was dealing with this matter that a distinction is made between need and effective demand. A married man surrounded by half a dozen children and living in two rooms may demonstrate to an investigator that he has a need for better housing conditions, but when you come to estimate his effective demand and find that he has not the money to put up for better rental premises or for the down payment on a new house, then you determine that he does not present any effective demand, and consequently does not affect the housing situation from that point of view. The minister may have a different interpretation of those words, but that was the way it was pointed out to me when I started to investigate housing.
It also seems to me, as was mentioned this afternoon, that sufficient emphasis has not been laid upon research to devise better and cheaper methods to erect houses in this country. Surely there is a great field there. In the 20 years that have elapsed, what has been done along that line? Mention has also been made of the advantage that would accrue if antiquated building restrictions were removed or modified to keep up with developments that have occurred in methods of constructing houses. That is tied in with the question of research. What is being done about that?
Scientifically, what is the backlog of housing in Canada? I think the minister used a figure of 100,000. Others say 500,000. Who knows? How do we determine it?

Why do we not know? Is there not some means of discovering not only the need but the effective demand for housing in Canada on a scientific basis?
Finally, when the minister was rewriting the act and bringing in the bill could he not have done something with parts II and III to correct their deficiencies? Have they met the need in Canada for low rental housing? Are these parts meeting the need for housing redevelopment, the so-called slum clearance?
If I have satisfied the minister with my introduction, Mr. Speaker, I should like to move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Churchill the debate was adjourned.
